tier_reason: The README of ashvardanian/ParallelReductionsBenchmark shows std::reduce<par> next to serial std::accumulate. The benchmark code is public (reduce_bench.cpp registering stl_par_reduce_gt and stl_accumulate_gt from reduce_cpu.hpp; Google Benchmark, MinTime 10 s, real time, result error checked). The README states GCC 12 and names the CPU (AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl), and CMakeLists.txt holds the flags. The runner is a third party, not Intel. The measured code is libstdc++'s bundled copy of Intel's Parallel STL on oneTBB, so the tie to this repository rests on lineage.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (stated in the README for the Graviton4 and Zen4 runs). CMake Release build: CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE becomes '-O3 -DNDEBUG -O2', and the last -O wins, so the build is -O2. For GNU compilers CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS to CMAKE_GCC_FLAGS ('-march=native -fopenmp'), so those flags do apply; tags v0.1.0, v0.2.0, v0.3.0, v0.4.0, v0.5.3 and HEAD v0.7.2 all use the same logic. oneTBB is fetched from uxlfoundation/oneTBB branch master (unpinned), and USE_INTEL_TBB defaults to ON on Linux without CUDA. Google Benchmark v1.9.1.
corrections.workload: Sum of a 1 GiB array of 268435456 floats, all set to 1.0f, using std::reduce(std::execution::par, first, last, T(0), std::plus<T>) versus serial std::accumulate, both from GCC 12's libstdc++. libstdc++'s <execution> uses its bundled Parallel STL with the oneTBB backend. The f64 rows accumulate the same float array into a double. Google Benchmark with MinTime 10 s and UseRealTime; the error is checked against the expected sum.
corrections.hardware: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl (Google Benchmark reports 96 x 2000 MHz; single NUMA node) for the headline row. AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl (192 x 3701.95 MHz reported; dual-socket per the README's observation; exact CPU SKU not stated) for the second row.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 777 stars and 122 forks on uxlfoundation/oneDPL, which github.com/intel/parallelstl now serves. Intel contributed its Parallel STL to GCC 9's libstdc++ as the implementation of the C++17 parallel algorithms (Phoronix 'GCC 9 libstdc++ Lands The C++17 Parallel Algorithms Implementation From Intel' and the gcc.gnu.org libstdc++ RFC of November 2017; WebSearch snippets only).
corrections.caveats: Indirect evidence: the benchmark runs libstdc++'s bundled <execution> implementation (a vendored copy of Intel's Parallel STL as contributed to GCC 9, backed by oneTBB). It does not build intel/parallelstl or oneDPL, and oneDPL's oneapi::dpl::execution policies were not measured. The baseline is a serial std::accumulate, whose strict left fold makes it latency-bound on the floating-point add chain, not memory-bound. On Graviton4 the single-thread unrolled/f32 loop (38034000 ns) is already 5.05x faster than std::accumulate/f32 (derived from page data), so 96-core parallelism accounts for only about 19.5x of the 98x (derived from page data). A std::reduce(seq) or unrolled serial baseline would show a far smaller gain. On Graviton4, hand-written OpenMP (neon/f32/openmp 1901684 ns) and fork_union (neon/f32/av::fork_union 1890173 ns; serial/f32/av::fork_union 1889686 ns) match or beat std::reduce<par>/f32 at 1950894 ns. The Graviton4 rows report 550 to 568 GB/s, above the 537.6 GB/s theoretical DRAM peak of one Graviton4 socket (12 channels of DDR5-5600; WikiChip and The Next Platform, snippet only). Repeated iterations over the 1 GiB buffer are therefore partly served from the 96 x 2 MB L2 and 36 MB L3, and absolute bandwidth is slightly inflated. std::accumulate<f32> shows 93.75 percent error because a float accumulator stops growing at 2^24; the f64 row is accurate. The README tables are single hand-pasted runs with no variance reported. oneTBB master is not pinned, and fork_union is fetched from its main branch. The benchmark repository has no LICENSE file. The DGX-H100 rows were not used: CUDA machines default USE_INTEL_TBB to OFF, so the backend is unclear, and that table's std::reduce<par, f64> and <par_unseq, f64> rows show error,%=100 (wrong result). The Zen4 table dates from the May 2024 README refresh and uses older row labels. The Graviton4 table was added in May 2025 and its std::reduce labels match the current reduce_bench.cpp. No comparison against MSVC STL, libc++ parallel algorithms or GNU parallel mode.

notes: Every claimed number matches the README exactly; the ratios are correctly marked as derived. The record's flag caveat was wrong: for GCC, CMakeLists.txt copies CMAKE_GCC_FLAGS into CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS, so -march=native -fopenmp do apply. Shortcomings to record: the measured code is libstdc++'s vendored Parallel STL rather than intel/parallelstl or oneDPL; the latency-bound serial baseline yields 5x from unrolling alone; fork_union and OpenMP match or beat it; oneTBB master is unpinned; reported bandwidth exceeds the DRAM peak; single runs; the benchmark repo has no license.
